records.our_prose: The maggots (young) of the cabbage maggot fly, a small gray fly. It spends the winter as pupae in the soil, and in spring the females lay tiny white eggs at the base of cabbage-family plants. The eggs hatch in about a week and the maggots burrow into the roots for three to four weeks. It goes after the whole cabbage family, turnips, radishes, cabbage, broccoli, and is worst in cool, damp spring weather.

records.our_prose: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows turnips on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs February 15 to March 1, the Group A (Hardy) date for St. George, with roots ready in about 50 days and the crop pulled by late April before the heat builds. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August, and USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table does not open the fall turnip window until July 1, so May and June together form a genuine bare-ground pause between the two cycles. The fall sowing runs July 1 to August 1, and USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area specifically groups turnips with carrots and beets as roots that hold well and can be dug quite late into winter, well past the November 1 average first frost.

Store roots only; use the greens fresh.

records.our_prose: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during germination and again as the roots size up. Turnip seed and seedlings need a moist, uncrusted surface for the roughly 7 to 10 days to emergence. Once established, turnips want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings.
